note: One paragraph per relation, written from the abstracts of the cited papers (arXiv metadata and Crossref checked 2026-10-06). Each claim about a result is attributed to the paper it comes from. Digitized or compared curves in sim-highline carry their own definitions; this text is context, not evidence.

gsmf.title: Stellar mass function
gsmf.paragraph: The galaxy stellar mass function counts galaxies per unit volume per dex of stellar mass and is the most basic census of how baryons have been turned into stars. Locally it is well described by a double Schechter function with a knee near 10^10.7 M☉ and an upturn at low mass (Baldry et al. 2012, building on earlier SDSS and 2MASS work such as Bell et al. 2003); deep surveys now trace it smoothly to z≈7.5, with the quiescent fraction and the cosmic stellar mass density evolving along with it (Weaver et al. 2023; Madau & Dickinson 2014 review the matching star-formation history). Simulations are usually tuned to it: EAGLE's feedback was calibrated to the z≈0 function and the model then tracks the observed evolution to z=7 within plausible observational uncertainty (Furlong et al. 2015), so agreement near z=0 is a calibration check, not a prediction. The informative tests are the low-mass slope (supernova feedback and resolution), the massive tail (AGN feedback, and how the mass of a central galaxy is defined: the diffuse-light fraction depends sensitively on aperture, Pillepich et al. 2018) and z>4, where JWST now constrains it. Check h-scalings, IMF and mass aperture before reading offsets as physics.

sfms.title: Star-forming main sequence
sfms.paragraph: The star-forming main sequence is the tight, nearly power-law correlation between star-formation rate and stellar mass among star-forming galaxies, and the observational backbone for how fast galaxies grow. Early surveys showed that it exists, that it sits at higher SFR at earlier times, and that star formation in most galaxies declines gradually after an initial onset (Noeske et al. 2007). Putting 25 studies on a common calibration, Speagle et al. (2014) found a consensus of about 0.1 dex between publications, an intrinsic width near 0.2 dex that does not change with cosmic time, and a slope that steepens toward early times; the most recent census to z≈6 finds curvature at high mass whose turnover mass tracks the halo mass at which accretion switches from cold to hot (Popesso et al. 2023). Simulations broadly reproduce the shape and scatter but disagree on normalisation at cosmic noon: Illustris matched z=0 and z=4 yet sat well below the data near z≈2 (Sparre et al. 2015); EAGLE's star-forming galaxies lie 0.2 to 0.4 dex below observed sSFRs while their evolution tracks the data (Furlong et al. 2015); for TNG the answer depends on the star-forming selection, the SFR timescale and the aperture (Donnari et al. 2019). Those systematics are as large as the offsets, so compare definitions before quoting a tension.

ssfr.title: Specific SFR
ssfr.paragraph: Specific star-formation rate, the SFR per unit stellar mass, is the inverse of a galaxy's mass-doubling time and is the main sequence viewed as a ratio. Observationally the sSFR of star-forming galaxies is close to constant with mass below a turnover mass and suppressed above it, and its normalisation rises steeply toward high redshift (Speagle et al. 2014; Popesso et al. 2023); the history this implies is a gradual decline rather than repeated bursts for most galaxies (Noeske et al. 2007), set against a cosmic SFR density that peaked near z≈2 (Madau & Dickinson 2014). In simulations sSFR is one of the least consistent outputs: EAGLE star-forming galaxies are 0.2 to 0.4 dex below observed values at fixed mass (Furlong et al. 2015), Illustris is too low near z≈2 (Sparre et al. 2015), and TNG values move by a comparable amount with the SFR timescale and aperture (Donnari et al. 2019). Physically, sSFR tracks the gas supply relative to the existing stars, so an offset points to gas accretion, gas fractions or feedback, but observed values also depend on the SFR indicator, the SED model and the IMF, which are not always converted. A threshold in sSFR is also what separates star-forming from quenched galaxies in many codes, which links sSFR tensions to quenched-fraction tensions.

mzr.title: Gas-phase mass–metallicity relation
mzr.paragraph: The mass–metallicity relation links a galaxy's stellar mass to the oxygen abundance of its star-forming gas. In about 53,000 SDSS galaxies it is tight (±0.1 dex), steep from 10^8.5 to 10^10.5 M☉ and flat above, which Tremonti et al. (2004) read as evidence that galactic winds remove metals most effectively from low-mass galaxies; at fixed mass it also depends on SFR (the fundamental metallicity relation, revisited on a Te-anchored scale by Curti et al. 2020). The absolute abundance scale is still uncertain: Te-based calibrations give a significantly lower normalisation than photoionisation-model ones (Curti et al. 2020), and the review by Maiolino & Mannucci (2019) lays out how the relation evolves with redshift and how it compares with models and simulations. IllustrisTNG reproduces the slope and the normalisation evolution at 0<z<2 over 10^9 to 10^10.5 M☉ and predicts a gradual decline at higher redshift (about −0.064 dex per unit z); the evolution is driven mainly by higher gas fractions, not by changes in metal retention, and most metals at z=0 lie outside the ISM (Torrey et al. 2019). FIRE zoom simulations also agree reasonably with the observed relation at z=0 to 3 and predict its evolution to z=6 in terms of gas and stellar mass fractions (Ma et al. 2016). Simulations report different tracers (O/H, Z/Z☉, metal mass fraction) and different gas selections, so sim-highline keeps them on separate axes and never mixes them.

zstar.title: Stellar mass–stellar metallicity relation
zstar.paragraph: The stellar mass–stellar metallicity relation traces the time-integrated enrichment of a galaxy's stars, so it responds more slowly than the gas-phase relation to recent accretion and outflows. From SDSS spectra, Gallazzi et al. (2005) found low-mass galaxies young and metal-poor and massive galaxies old and metal-rich, with a rapid change at intermediate mass; resolved-star spectroscopy shows that dwarf irregulars and dwarf spheroidals follow one relation, Z★ ∝ M★^0.30, roughly continuous with galaxies up to 10^12 M☉ (Kirby et al. 2013). The chemical-evolution review of Maiolino & Mannucci (2019) stresses that stellar and gas-phase metallicities carry complementary information and compares both with simulations. Simulations predict the same positive trend: FIRE zoom simulations agree reasonably with the observed relations at z=0 to 3 and predict stellar metallicity rising with mass with a slope near 0.40 and a normalisation that declines with redshift, linked to the evolution of stellar and gas mass fractions (Ma et al. 2016). Absolute values nevertheless depend on the assumed yields, on whether metallicity is mass- or light-weighted, on the aperture and on the adopted solar abundance, which in this data well ranges from 0.0127 to 0.0142, so slope and evolution are safer comparisons than normalisation. Observational values come from a mix of absorption-line indices and full spectral fitting with different age–metallicity degeneracies.

size.title: Mass–size relation
size.paragraph: The size–mass relation says that more massive galaxies are larger, with different slopes and zero points for star-forming and quiescent systems. SDSS showed that late-type sizes scale as M^0.15 below about 10^10.6 M☉ and as M^0.4 above, with early types steeper at M^0.55 (Shen et al. 2003); HST surveys then established that quiescent galaxies were much more compact at high redshift, with R_eff ∝ (1+z)^−1.48 against (1+z)^−0.75 for star-forming galaxies (van der Wel et al. 2014), and that the median size of the most massive galaxies keeps evolving out to z≈3 (Mowla et al. 2019); Conselice (2014) reviews the structural evolution behind this. EAGLE agrees with observations to about 0.1 dex at z<1 and 0.2 to 0.3 dex at 1<z<2, with passive galaxies smaller than active ones at fixed mass (Furlong et al. 2017); TNG100 reproduces the trends and matches projected r-band sizes within 0.25 dex over 0<z<2, and shows quenched galaxies hardly growing in size before they quench while main-sequence galaxies grow steadily (Genel et al. 2018). Size growth therefore records accretion of angular momentum, mergers and the timing of quenching. Beware the definition: 3D half-mass radii and projected half-light radii (which depend on wavelength) differ by tenths of a dex, and sim-highline refuses to score one against the other.

refs.cite: van der Wel et al. 2014, ApJ 788, 28

shmr.title: Stellar–halo mass relation
shmr.paragraph: The stellar-to-halo mass relation measures how efficiently halos have converted baryons into stars. Abundance matching and its descendants (Behroozi et al. 2013; Moster et al. 2013) found a relation sharply peaked near halo masses of 10^12 M☉ that changes with redshift; the review by Wechsler & Tinker (2018) concludes that galaxy-formation efficiency is a strong function of halo mass and that the galaxy–halo connection is both a key test of galaxy formation models and an input to cosmological constraints. UniverseMachine ties galaxy growth to halo assembly and finds that quenching at z>1 correlates strongly with halo mass (Behroozi et al. 2019). At the massive end the observations themselves are uncertain: brightest-cluster-galaxy stellar masses scale as M500^0.35, and earlier abundance-matching results underestimated them by factors of 2 to 4 because the photometry missed outer light (Kravtsov et al. 2018). Simulations are partly calibrated to the relation and then differ in detail: in TNG the 3D stellar mass within 30 kpc scales as M500c^0.49 with 0.12 dex scatter, and the diffuse-light fraction depends strongly on how a central galaxy's mass is defined (Pillepich et al. 2018). The halo-mass definition (M200c, Bryan–Norman virial, FOF) and the stellar aperture each shift curves by amounts that rival differences between models.

bh.title: Black hole–stellar mass relation
bh.paragraph: The black hole–stellar mass relation connects the mass of a galaxy's central black hole to the total stellar mass of its host, and is the main constraint on how black holes grow relative to their galaxies. Dynamical masses show that black holes correlate with bulges but weakly with disks and halos, which Kormendy & Ho (2013) take as evidence against simple coevolution; broad-line AGN samples extend the relation to lower-mass hosts (Reines & Volonteri 2015), and searches for intermediate-mass black holes suggest that many 10^9 to 10^10 M☉ galaxies host black holes below 10^5 M☉, with the relation continuing at large scatter (Greene et al. 2020). Simulations differ strongly in black-hole seeding and in their supernova and AGN feedback. Habouzit et al. (2021) compare Illustris, TNG100, TNG300, Horizon-AGN, EAGLE and SIMBA and find that all produce tight relations but struggle to make black holes below 10^7.5 M☉ in galaxies of 10^10.5 to 10^11.5 M☉, that the mean relation evolves mildly (under 1 dex in black-hole mass for 0<z<5) with code-dependent shape and normalisation, and that supernova feedback strength shapes the relation below 10^10.5 M☉. Observed samples are subject to selection effects (resolving the sphere of influence, AGN luminosity), so compare like with like.

bhsigma.title: Black hole–velocity dispersion (M–σ)
bhsigma.paragraph: The M–σ relation links black-hole mass to the stellar velocity dispersion of the host bulge, and is the tightest of the black-hole scaling relations. Two groups established it in 2000 with slopes that did not initially agree (M ∝ σ^4.8 for Ferrarese & Merritt 2000; M ∝ σ^3.75 with 0.30 dex scatter for Gebhardt et al. 2000). The review by Kormendy & Ho (2013) places it in a picture where black holes correlate best with bulge properties; van den Bosch (2016) finds M ∝ σ^5.4 and shows the relation is an edge-on view of a plane involving black-hole mass, galaxy mass and size; and at the low-mass end it appears to continue unbroken to about 10^5 M☉ with large scatter (Greene et al. 2020). Simulations rarely compute σ the way observers measure it, so comparisons depend on the aperture, weighting and projection used, and several codes were calibrated to a black-hole–bulge or black-hole–stellar mass relation rather than to M–σ (Habouzit et al. 2021). Physically, a tight M–σ is read as regulation of black-hole growth by the depth of the central potential, but selection effects and the unresolved sphere of influence matter for both data and models. sim-highline stores the dispersion definition per record and refuses to rank across different ones.

jstar.title: Stellar specific angular momentum–mass relation
jstar.paragraph: The specific angular momentum–mass relation, the Fall relation, ties the angular momentum per unit mass of a galaxy's stars to its stellar mass. In ΛCDM, tidal torques give halos j ∝ M^(2/3), so disks that retain their angular momentum should follow that slope; observations show parallel tracks for ellipticals and spirals, with ellipticals holding about 3 to 4 times less (Romanowsky & Fall 2012), and the SPARC rotation-curve sample now defines the relation for spirals over 10^7 to 10^11.5 M☉ (Posti et al. 2018). Simulations reproduce the broad picture: Illustris galaxies fall on two relations, with late types retaining essentially all the angular momentum from cosmological torques and early types about 30% (Genel et al. 2015); Magneticum disk and spheroid galaxies compare well with observations (Teklu et al. 2015); and EAGLE agrees at z=0, with a scatter that correlates with morphology proxies such as gas fraction and stellar concentration (Lagos et al. 2017). Reviews of galaxy-formation models find a remarkable convergence between methods on a core set of processes (cosmological accretion, strong stellar-driven winds that are more efficient at low mass, and black-hole feedback that suppresses star formation at high mass), and angular momentum is the structural property that depends most directly on how that gas is accreted and removed (Somerville & Davé 2015). The measurement radius (r50 versus total), the mass range above the resolution limit and the morphological sample change j substantially, so curves from different papers are not interchangeable without checking those choices.

quenched.title: Quenched fraction
quenched.paragraph: The quenched fraction records the growth of the red sequence as a function of mass and epoch. The colour bimodality of galaxies was quantified in SDSS by Baldry et al. (2004); Peng et al. (2010) showed that the effects of stellar mass and of environment on the quiescent fraction are separable to z≈1, with mass quenching proportional to star-formation rate; Weaver et al. (2023) trace the quiescent fraction to z≈7.5; and Man & Belli (2018) review how star formation shuts off in massive galaxies, concluding that there is still no consensus on the mechanism. Simulations are tested hard on this relation because it depends on feedback. For TNG about 80% of 10^10.5 to 10^11 M☉ galaxies are quiescent at z=0 and about 50% at z=2 (Donnari et al. 2019), and the quenched fraction of massive centrals and satellites changes by up to 70% and 30% respectively with the quenching definition alone, and by up to about 50% with the SFR aperture (Donnari et al. 2021). Because those analysis choices matter as much as the physics, sim-highline stores the quenching criterion and refuses to compare different ones; most current codes quench massive galaxies with AGN feedback, which is exactly what this relation constrains.

gas.title: Cold gas fraction
gas.paragraph: The cold gas fraction gives the mass of cold gas, atomic plus molecular, per unit stellar mass. Local surveys (COLD GASS and xGASS) showed that gas fractions fall with stellar mass, that atomic fractions keep rising down to 10^9 M☉ with no plateau, and that total reservoirs stay HI-dominated across 10^9 to 10^11.5 M☉ (Saintonge et al. 2011; Catinella et al. 2018; reviewed by Saintonge & Catinella 2022). At higher redshift, star-forming galaxies contained far more molecular gas and have shorter depletion times, set by redshift and by distance from the main sequence (Tacconi et al. 2020). Simulations must post-process gas into HI and H2, which makes the relation partly a test of that step: EAGLE reproduces the observed H2 scaling relations and a rising H2 fraction toward high redshift (Lagos et al. 2015), standard-resolution EAGLE under-produces HI in galaxies below 10^10 M☉ unless the resolution is raised (Crain et al. 2017), and IllustrisTNG agrees broadly with local gas fractions (Diemer et al. 2019). Physically the relation constrains accretion, feedback and the conversion of gas to stars. In this data well the gas relation mixes several definitions (HI+H2, cold gas above a density cut, different apertures), recorded in each record's definitions.

hi-fraction.title: HI gas fraction
hi-fraction.paragraph: The HI-to-stellar mass fraction measures the atomic gas reservoir relative to the stars, and is what 21 cm surveys measure directly. xGASS finds that HI fractions keep rising with decreasing stellar mass with no plateau down to 10^9 M☉, and that total gas reservoirs stay HI-dominated (Catinella et al. 2018); the review of Saintonge & Catinella (2022) places this within the network of gas scaling relations and their links to morphology and star formation. EAGLE's reference-resolution run is HI-deficient in galaxies below 10^10 M☉ while higher-resolution runs largely are not, and at fixed stellar mass the HI content evolves strongly with redshift (Crain et al. 2017); IllustrisTNG, post-processed with a separate HI/H2 framework, agrees well with observed gas fractions at z≈0 (Diemer et al. 2019). Physically, HI traces gas that has neither been converted to molecular gas, consumed, nor expelled, so the relation constrains accretion, the neutral–molecular split, and stellar and AGN feedback. The median depends on detection limits and on the radius within which HI is summed (70 pkpc in the EAGLE work), which each record states.

h2-fraction.title: H2 gas fraction
h2-fraction.paragraph: The H2-to-stellar mass fraction is the star-forming gas reservoir relative to the stars and, with the depletion time, sets how long a galaxy can keep forming stars at its current rate. Local CO surveys (COLD GASS) found that the molecular content depends on structure, with sharp thresholds in properties such as stellar surface density (Saintonge et al. 2011); at higher redshift star-forming galaxies held much more molecular gas, with depletion times set by redshift and distance from the main sequence (Tacconi et al. 2020). In simulations H2 is assigned in post-processing, so the result depends on the prescription: Lagos et al. (2015) show that two prescriptions in EAGLE reproduce the observed scaling relations with stellar mass, SFR and surface density, with larger H2 fractions and shorter depletion times at high redshift; Diemer et al. (2019) find that TNG compares well with observations and that H2 mass correlates with SFR with an almost constant depletion time. Detection-limited samples, such as COLD GASS with M★>10^10 M☉ and CO above a limit, are not all-galaxy medians; the selection is stated in the relevant records.

btfr.title: Baryonic Tully–Fisher relation
btfr.paragraph: The baryonic Tully–Fisher relation says that the baryonic mass, stars plus gas, of a rotationally supported galaxy scales tightly with its rotation velocity, roughly as V^4. McGaugh et al. (2000) showed that the optical relation breaks for low-velocity, gas-rich galaxies but that one linear relation is restored once gas is included. With the SPARC sample, Lelli et al. (2019) find that the tightest relation uses the mean velocity along the flat part of the rotation curve, with slope 3.85±0.09 (3.5 to 4.0 allowing for systematics) and an orthogonal intrinsic scatter of only 6%. Simulations are tested on the slope and scatter because these probe feedback and halo response: NIHAO galaxies reproduce the observed inefficiency of galaxy formation through the stellar, gas and baryonic relations, with scatter of 0.08 to 0.14 dex for HI velocities of 70 to 220 km/s (Dutton et al. 2017), and EAGLE spirals show a tight mass–velocity scaling provided disk sizes satisfy constraints set by halo concentration and response (Ferrero et al. 2017). The velocity definition (flat rotation speed, line width, halo Vmax) changes the slope more than differences between models do, and several records here are zoom samples that are not volume complete. Reviews of mass estimators (Courteau et al. 2014) stress that stellar-population masses and dynamical masses each carry their own systematic uncertainties.

refs.cite: Courteau et al. 2014, Rev. Mod. Phys. 86, 47

stfr.title: Stellar-mass Tully–Fisher relation
stfr.paragraph: The stellar-mass Tully–Fisher relation is the Tully–Fisher relation with stellar mass in place of luminosity, so its slope and scatter depend on the stellar mass-to-light ratios used: Bell & de Jong (2001) showed that these vary by factors of 3 to 7 in the optical and, under a universal IMF, argued for a stellar IMF with fewer low-mass stars than Salpeter. McGaugh et al. (2000) found that the stellar relation breaks at low velocity because faint galaxies are gas dominated, which is why the baryonic version is preferred. NIHAO simulations reproduce the stellar relation with small scatter for HI velocities of 70 to 220 km/s (Dutton et al. 2017), and EAGLE spirals follow a tight mass–velocity scaling that can be reconciled with abundance matching only if disk sizes follow halo concentration and response (Ferrero et al. 2017). The relation tests the fraction of baryons locked into stars at fixed halo velocity and therefore the efficiency of feedback; because it ignores gas it is more sensitive to galaxy selection than the baryonic relation. Reviews of mass estimators (Courteau et al. 2014) stress the same point for stellar-population masses in general. The IMF assumption alone shifts the zero point by up to about 0.2 dex (Salpeter versus Chabrier).

refs.cite: Courteau et al. 2014, Rev. Mod. Phys. 86, 47

mzrz.variantNote: Shown here as log(Z/Z☉); the solar scale (Z☉) differs between sources.

uvlf.title: UV luminosity function
uvlf.paragraph: The rest-frame UV luminosity function counts galaxies per unit comoving volume per magnitude of absolute UV magnitude. It is the most direct census of unobscured star formation at high redshift, which is why JWST analyses report it before any stellar-mass relation. It is usually fitted with a Schechter function; HST data show a smooth flattening of the faint-end slope from about -2.4 at z~10 to -1.5 at z~2 and a monotonic rise of the normalisation towards lower redshift (Bouwens et al. 2021). JWST extends the measurement to z~9-16: Harikane et al. 2023 find the star-formation rate density at z~12-16 above a constant star-formation-efficiency model, whereas Donnan et al. 2024 conclude that the evolution to z~12 can be reproduced in LCDM with younger stellar populations and no change in dust or efficiency. Simulations can be compared only after fixing the dust treatment, because intrinsic and attenuated functions differ most at the bright end: THESAN applies a dust-attenuation model and broadly matches the observed z=6-10 functions (Kannan et al. 2022), FLARES publishes dust-attenuated and intrinsic functions at z=10-15, so the JWST counts can be compared on either footing (Wilkins et al. 2023), FIRE-2 attributes the z~6 decline brighter than M1500~-20 largely to dust (Ma et al. 2018), and at the faint end the predictions follow the halo mass function and the resolution limit. Madau & Dickinson 2014 give the longer view of the star-formation history this function feeds.

uvbeta.title: UV continuum slope against UV magnitude
uvbeta.paragraph: The UV continuum slope beta is the power-law index of a galaxy's rest-frame ultraviolet light, f_lambda proportional to lambda^beta, plotted here against absolute UV magnitude. In local starbursts it tracks the dust attenuation (Meurer et al. 1999), which is why the review of Madau & Dickinson (2014) uses it to correct UV luminosity densities for dust. At redshifts 4 to 8 brighter galaxies are redder: Bouwens et al. (2014) find d beta / d M_UV of about -0.1 to -0.2 per magnitude from HST broad-band fluxes, and Topping et al. (2024) find slopes of -0.06 to -0.12 with JWST at median redshifts 5.9 to 9.4. Simulations with dust give a similar trend whose size depends on the dust law: Shen et al. (2020) find IllustrisTNG flatter than observed, too blue at the bright end, and Wu et al. (2020) find that SIMBA with a Calzetti law agrees with the observations at z = 6 while an SMC law is about 0.4 too red. With no dust the simulated slope is flat, near -2.1 to -2.4, so most of the trend in these models is dust. A comparison is fair only when the dust treatment (attenuated or intrinsic), the way beta is measured (a power law through chosen filters or through a wavelength window) and the magnitude and galaxies used all match; each record states these as its paper does, and a value the paper does not give stays unspecified and is not counted as a match.

uvbetam.title: UV continuum slope against stellar mass
uvbetam.paragraph: The same slope beta, the index of f_lambda proportional to lambda^beta in the rest-frame ultraviolet, can be plotted against stellar mass instead of UV magnitude. Because beta follows the dust attenuation in starbursts (Meurer et al. 1999) and the mass-metallicity relation links mass to dust, more massive galaxies are expected to be redder. Finkelstein et al. (2012) measured the median beta in three bins of stellar mass from log M of 7 to 10 at redshifts 4 to 8 and found redder slopes at higher mass, with slopes of 0.17 to 0.46 per dex at z = 4 to 7; they caution that low-mass red galaxies are harder to detect and that masses from rest-UV photometry alone are uncertain. Wu et al. (2020) compare SIMBA at z = 6 with those points and note that the observations indicate much steeper changes of beta with stellar mass than the simulation gives. The review of Madau & Dickinson (2014) discusses the slope as a dust correction in the cosmic star formation history. Records here differ in how mass is obtained (an SED fit to rest-UV photometry in the observations, the galaxy's star particles in the simulation), in the dust treatment and in how beta is measured, and these must match before an offset between a simulation and the data is read as physics.

sfrd.title: Cosmic star-formation rate density
sfrd.paragraph: The cosmic star-formation rate density is the star-formation rate summed over all galaxies per unit comoving volume, plotted against redshift. Observationally it rises to a peak near z~2 and declines by about an order of magnitude to the present; the standard compilation of UV and infrared surveys and its fitting function is Madau & Dickinson 2014, which assumes a Salpeter IMF. At z>8 only UV estimates exist and they depend on the dust correction and on how far down the luminosity function is integrated: Harikane et al. 2023 find a decline from z~9 to 12 and perhaps 16, and Donnan et al. 2024 confirm a gradual decline out to z~12. In simulations it is the least ambiguous quantity to extract, but it integrates over everything including galaxies below any observational limit. ASTRID shows a whole-box total and a subset above 0.3 solar masses per year that diverge at high redshift (Bird et al. 2022), THESAN runs of lower resolution lose an order of magnitude at z>10 because they miss low-mass halos (Kannan et al. 2022), and EAGLE follows the observed shape but lies below the compilation near the peak, which is why the paper also plots the curve raised by 0.2 dex (Furlong et al. 2015). Convert to a common IMF before reading offsets as physics.

smd.title: Cosmic stellar mass density
smd.paragraph: The cosmic stellar mass density is the stellar mass summed over all galaxies per unit comoving volume, plotted against redshift. Because stars only accumulate, it is essentially the time integral of the cosmic star-formation rate density minus the mass returned by evolved stars, so it rises steadily from high redshift to today. The standard observational reference is the compilation of Madau & Dickinson 2014, who show that the integral of their star-formation history, reduced for stellar mass loss, matches the measured densities. In simulations the quantity depends on which galaxies are counted: FIREbox shows both all identified galaxies and only those above 10^9.3 solar masses, and the two differ most at high redshift where low-mass galaxies hold much of the mass (Feldmann et al. 2023). Zoom volumes such as NewHorizon give the density of the refined region, not a cosmic average (Dubois et al. 2021). Read offsets only after converting to a common IMF and checking whether the density is per comoving or physical volume.

sfrf.title: Star-formation rate function
sfrf.paragraph: The star-formation rate function is the number of galaxies per unit comoving volume per dex of star-formation rate. It is the SFR counterpart of the stellar mass function and the distribution whose integral weighted by SFR gives the cosmic star-formation rate density (Madau & Dickinson 2014), so it shows which galaxies build the stellar mass of the Universe at each epoch. Observed functions are derived from dust-corrected UV luminosity functions, infrared luminosity functions or H-alpha surveys: Smit et al. (2012) convert the z=4 to 7 UV luminosity functions with dust corrections based on the UV slope and the IRX-beta relation, and find a characteristic SFR that grows from about 5 solar masses per year at z~8 to about 100 at z~2. Each tracer has its own calibration (Kennicutt & Evans 2012), and they do not always agree: Katsianis et al. (2017) compile UV, IR and H-alpha functions and find them inconsistent for the highest star-forming objects at z<2, possibly through selection biases and dust attenuation. In EAGLE supernova feedback sets the abundance of galaxies at all star-forming regimes while AGN feedback affects only the highest-SFR systems (Katsianis et al. 2017), and at z~4 to 7 the function is insensitive to feedback at z>5 but responds to it at lower redshift (Tescari et al. 2014). Two curves are comparable only if the SFR indicator and dust correction, the IMF, the SFR timescale and the comoving normalisation per dex agree.

himf.title: HI mass function
himf.paragraph: The HI mass function counts galaxies per unit comoving volume per dex of atomic-hydrogen mass, and its integral is the cosmic HI density. It is measured directly from blind 21 cm surveys that do not depend on optical selection. The HIPASS Bright Galaxy Catalogue of 1000 galaxies gave a Schechter function with faint-end slope -1.30 and a cosmic HI density of (3.8±0.6)×10^-4, with later-type galaxies having steeper slopes (Zwaan et al. 2003). The final ALFALFA catalogue gives a knee mass of 10^9.94 and a low-mass slope of -1.25, and its authors conclude that the knee is a fair cosmological measurement while the slope is representative only of the local Universe (Jones et al. 2018). The review of the cold interstellar medium by Saintonge & Catinella (2022) places the function within the network of gas scaling relations. Simulations must assign HI in post-processing, so the function tests that step as much as the physics. In EAGLE the standard-resolution run underestimates HI column densities, which leaves a deficiency below 10^10 M☉ and a poor match to the observed function; higher-resolution runs largely remove this (Crain et al. 2017). TNG agrees well for gas fractions but overestimates the total neutral gas abundance at z=0 by about a factor of two (Diemer et al. 2019), and Simba, EAGLE and TNG all qualitatively reproduce the local function while diverging in its evolution to z~2 (Davé et al. 2020). Compare curves only after matching the HI definition (self-shielding and molecular correction, aperture), the h-scaling of masses and volumes, and the comoving normalisation.

hmf.title: Halo mass function
hmf.paragraph: The halo mass function is the comoving number density of dark-matter haloes per dex of halo mass. It is the starting point of every galaxy-halo model: abundance matching and semi-analytic models assume it, and the baseline against which galaxy abundances are read as efficiencies. It is fixed by cosmology and the growth of structure, but only for a stated mass definition: Tinker et al. (2008) calibrated it in collisionless simulations to about 5% for 10^11 to 10^15 M☉/h, argued that spherical-overdensity masses are more directly linked to cluster observables than friends-of-friends masses, and found that no universal fitting function holds at that accuracy, with the amplitude falling by 20 to 50% from z=0 to 2.5 depending on the mass definition. Cluster counts anchor the massive end: Chandra measurements of the mass function at z≈0.05 and z≈0.55 give cosmological constraints (Vikhlinin et al. 2009). Baryons modify the function: in Magneticum they lower cluster masses and so reduce number densities at fixed mass, an effect that vanishes at z~2 and above 10^14 M☉ (Bocquet et al. 2016), and galaxy formation lowers it by about 20%, in correction formulae derived from simulations that reproduce the observed baryon fractions (Velliscig et al. 2014). Frenk & White (2012) review the role of simulations in this picture. Curves are comparable only if the halo mass definition (M200c, M200m, M500c, virial, FOF), the cosmology and h-units, the comoving normalisation per dex, and the choice of dark-matter-only or hydrodynamical masses agree.

dmf.title: Dust mass function
dmf.paragraph: The dust mass function counts galaxies per unit comoving volume per dex of dust mass. Its integral is the cosmic dust density, and its shape constrains how dust is produced, grown and destroyed. Locally, the GAMA/H-ATLAS function of 15,750 galaxies at z<0.1 is a Schechter function with a faint-end slope of 1.22 and a dust density parameter of 1.1×10^-6 integrated down to 10^4 M☉ (Beeston et al. 2018). The Herschel-ATLAS found rapid evolution of dust in galaxies over the past 5 Gyr (Dunne et al. 2011), and Pozzi et al. (2020) extended the function to z≈2.5 and found a broad peak of the dust mass density near z≈1. The review by Galliano et al. (2018) covers the dust properties of nearby galaxies from which such masses are inferred. Simulations do not agree with each other: a smoothed-particle simulation with a dust-evolution model reproduces the z=0 function but overproduces dust masses above 10^8 M☉ (Hou et al. 2019); Simba reproduces it at z=0 but falls short by about a factor of three at z~1 to 2 (Li et al. 2019); and IllustrisTNG, post-processed with a dust model, shows no evolution of the function at 0<z<0.5, in conflict with the rapid evolution derived from observations (Millard et al. 2020). Observed dust masses depend on the spectral-energy-distribution model (single or multiple temperatures, energy balance) and on the dust absorption coefficient, simulated ones on the dust model or post-processing recipe, and the units carry h factors, so compare only matched definitions and the comoving normalisation per dex.

dtg.title: Dust-to-gas ratio
dtg.paragraph: The dust-to-gas ratio is the dust mass divided by the atomic plus molecular gas mass of a galaxy, plotted against its gas-phase oxygen abundance, 12+log(O/H). It measures what fraction of the metals is locked in grains, so it tests models of dust production, growth and destruction. In the SINGS galaxies the ratio depends on metallicity, with spirals resembling the dust of the local Milky Way (Draine et al. 2007). A sample of 126 local galaxies spanning 2 dex in metallicity shows that metallicity is the property that drives the ratio among five tested, that the relation is not a single power law of slope -1, and that it is steeper below 12+log(O/H)≈8.0, with a scatter of 0.37 dex at fixed metallicity (Rémy-Ruyer et al. 2014). The review by Galliano et al. (2018) surveys the dust properties of nearby galaxies behind these numbers. Simulations with dust models can match the local trend: one cosmological model reproduces the observed relation for nearby galaxies (Aoyama et al. 2018), another agrees with it at z=0 (Hou et al. 2019), and Simba predicts a tight positive correlation for star-forming galaxies that is absent for quenched ones, with little evolution between z=0 and 6 (Li et al. 2019). Observed ratios depend on the molecular gas mass, which Rémy-Ruyer et al. (2014) derive with either a Galactic or a metallicity-dependent CO conversion factor, and on the dust-mass method and the oxygen-abundance calibration, so curves are comparable only with matched gas definitions.

metald.title: Cosmic metal mass density
metald.paragraph: The cosmic metal mass density is the mass of heavy elements per unit comoving volume as a function of redshift. Because stars only add metals, it follows the integrated star-formation history, but where the metals sit changes with time. Madau & Dickinson (2014) review how the history of star formation and of heavy-element production can be mapped from the cosmic dark ages to today. Péroux & Howk (2020) compile contemporary censuses of the baryons and metals in collapsed structures and conclude that cold gas contains virtually all the metals produced by stars at z>2.5, whereas at z<1 most of the observed metals are bound in stars. At z~0, only 20 to 25% of the metals produced by galaxies of 10^9.3 to 10^11.6 M☉ remain in their stars, interstellar gas and dust, and the bulk lie outside them (Peeples et al. 2014). A simulation comparison must therefore be made phase by phase: Yates et al. (2021) contrast damped Lyman-alpha observations with L-Galaxies, TNG100 and EAGLE, and find that the fraction of metals in neutral gas is below 40% at 3<z<5 in all three while the observations suggest above 85%, with hot, low-density gas a major contributor to the metal budget even at high redshift. The two EAGLE curves in this data well, summed over all gas particles and over all star particles, are different pieces of that budget and are never interchangeable. Compare only the same metal phase (all gas, neutral gas, stars or total), the comoving frame, and the IMF and yields behind the metal production.

age.title: Stellar age–mass relation
age.paragraph: The age relation gives the typical age of the stars in a galaxy as a function of stellar mass, and so records how long star formation lasted. From SDSS spectra Gallazzi et al. (2005) derived light-weighted ages and found low-mass galaxies young and massive galaxies old, with a rapid transition between the two regimes. Mattolini et al. (2025) revise this with updated population synthesis models and aperture corrections, and find a bimodal mass-age distribution with a young and an old sequence that transition at 10^10.8 M☉; their aperture corrections lower masses, ages and metallicities in a mass-dependent way. For early-type galaxies, spectral fitting gives mass-weighted ages and star-formation histories whose duration is longer in lower-mass objects (McDermid et al. 2015). Conroy (2013) reviews what can be measured from galaxy spectral energy distributions, including star-formation histories, metallicities and the initial mass function. Simulations do not provide ages the way observers measure them, so tests are indirect: Hill et al. (2017) compare the time at which half of the stellar mass was assembled with the median light-weighted ages of SDSS galaxies, find that both correlate strongly with mass in the data, and report that EAGLE instead shows a flat relation between assembly time and mass, which the semi-analytic model they test reproduces. A curve is comparable only if the age weighting (light or mass, and the band), the stellar mass definition and aperture, the IMF and the population synthesis model all agree.

bhmd.title: Cosmic black-hole mass density
bhmd.paragraph: The cosmic black-hole mass density is the mass in supermassive black holes per unit comoving volume, plotted against redshift. Observationally it is built in two ways that must agree: from the local black-hole mass function, and by integrating the accretion implied by AGN luminosity functions for an assumed radiative efficiency. Yu & Tremaine (2002) combined SDSS velocity dispersions with the black hole mass-dispersion relation to estimate a local density of 2.5×10^5 M☉ Mpc^-3, consistent with the density accreted during optically bright quasar phases for an efficiency of 0.1. Marconi et al. (2004) found 4.6×10^5 (h/0.7)^2 M☉ Mpc^-3 and an anti-hierarchical growth in which smaller black holes grow later. Shankar et al. (2009) show that local estimates still span 3 to 5.5×10^5 M☉ Mpc^-3 and that the integrated AGN emissivity closely tracks the cosmic star-formation history, which Heckman & Best (2014) review in the wider context of galaxy and black-hole co-evolution. In simulations the density is the integral of the black-hole mass function: Habouzit et al. (2021) find that Illustris, TNG100, TNG300, Horizon-AGN, EAGLE and SIMBA struggle to form black holes below 10^7.5 M☉ in galaxies of 10^10.5 to 10^11.5 M☉ and, compared with local observations, produce an excess of black holes above 10^9 M☉ in most cases. Because observed densities rest on the assumed efficiency and the mass scale of the M-sigma relation and carry h factors, compare curves only with the same black-hole mass method, comoving frame and cosmology.

fgas500.title: Hot gas fraction within R500
fgas500.paragraph: The gas fraction within R500 is the mass of hot, X-ray emitting gas divided by the total mass inside the radius that encloses 500 times the critical density, plotted against M500c and here normalised by the cosmic baryon fraction. It records how much of the infalling gas feedback has expelled, so it constrains supernova and AGN feedback at group masses. Vikhlinin et al. (2006) measured gas and hydrostatic total-mass profiles for 13 relaxed clusters with Chandra, and Lovisari et al. (2015) used XMM-Newton observations of a complete group sample and, with a master sample of 82 objects spanning two orders of magnitude in mass, found almost a factor of two difference in gas mass fraction between groups and clusters. The mass estimator matters: with weak-lensing-calibrated masses the XXL clusters have gas fractions substantially lower than those found with hydrostatic masses, a baryon budget short of the cosmic value by about a factor of two at R500, and a hydrostatic bias of 1-b=0.72 (Eckert et al. 2016). Kravtsov & Borgani (2012) review gas and stellar fractions as a testing ground for galaxy formation models. In cosmo-OWLS some AGN feedback models give a realistic population of groups and clusters while others are too violent (Le Brun et al. 2014), BAHAMAS calibrates its feedback to the hot gas mass fractions of groups and clusters (McCarthy et al. 2017), and the C-EAGLE clusters are too gas rich (Barnes et al. 2017). Compare only the same aperture, normalisation, and mass method, and whether a simulated mass is true or X-ray-estimated.

fmr.title: Fundamental metallicity relation
fmr.paragraph: The fundamental metallicity relation extends the mass-metallicity relation by a dependence on star-formation rate: at fixed stellar mass, galaxies with higher SFR have lower gas-phase oxygen abundance. It is usually shown as a projection, mu_alpha = log M★ - alpha log SFR, against 12+log(O/H). Mannucci et al. (2010) found a tight surface in stellar mass, SFR and metallicity with a residual dispersion of about 0.05 dex, adopted alpha=0.32 as the value that minimises the local scatter, and found that galaxies out to z≈2.5 follow it. The projection is not universal: direct-method stacks of about 200,000 SDSS galaxies show a factor of two to three greater dependence on SFR than strong-line studies (Andrews & Martini 2013), and a fully Te-anchored recalibration lowers the normalisation and gives a new parametrisation (Curti et al. 2020). MOSDEF finds no evidence that the relation evolves out to z≈3.3 (Sanders et al. 2021), and Maiolino & Mannucci (2019) review the chemical evolution behind it. The simulated relation in EAGLE agrees remarkably well with the observed one at z≲5 (De Rossi et al. 2017), whereas TNG50 and MaNGA both indicate that galaxy size is a stronger secondary parameter than SFR (Ma et al. 2024). Curves are comparable only if alpha, the metallicity quantity and calibration (strong-line, Te-anchored or intrinsic simulation abundance), the SFR indicator and timescale, the IMF and the mass definition are matched.

ks.title: Kennicutt–Schmidt relation
ks.paragraph: The Kennicutt-Schmidt relation links the surface density of star formation to the surface density of gas, and it is the empirical law that star-formation prescriptions in galaxy-formation models try to reproduce. Kennicutt (1998) combined 61 normal spirals with 36 infrared-selected starbursts and found that disk-averaged SFR and gas densities follow a Schmidt law with index 1.4±0.15 over several orders of magnitude. At sub-kpc resolution in 18 nearby galaxies, Bigiel et al. (2008) found instead that the SFR surface density is linear (index 1.0±0.2) in the H2 surface density, with a depletion time of about 2 Gyr, while in most galaxies HI correlates little or not at all with SFR. Leroy et al. (2013) found a similar molecular depletion time at 1 kpc resolution with systematic second-order variations, which a CO-to-H2 conversion factor that depends on the dust-to-gas ratio can explain, though not uniquely. Kennicutt & Evans (2012) review the relation from entire galaxies to individual clouds and provide updated SFR prescriptions. In the FIRE simulations the relation emerges from feedback regulation and is independent of redshift and averaging scale, but the cold and dense gas surface density is about 0.5 dex lower than observed at kpc scales (Orr et al. 2018), and in IllustrisTNG the H2 mass correlates with SFR with an almost constant depletion time (Diemer et al. 2019). Curves are comparable only if the gas (total, HI+H2 or H2), the averaging scale (pixel size or galaxy-integrated), the SFR indicator and timescale, the IMF and the CO conversion factor agree.

sigmam.title: Stellar mass–velocity dispersion relation
sigmam.paragraph: This relation links a galaxy's stellar mass to its central stellar velocity dispersion, an observable that reflects the depth of the central gravitational potential (it is not the black-hole M-sigma relation). For massive quiescent galaxies at z<0.7, Zahid et al. (2016) find that the relation and its scatter are independent of redshift, with sigma proportional to M^0.3 above 10^10.3 M☉, the same slope as the halo mass to dark-matter velocity dispersion relation of N-body simulations; they suggest that the central stellar dispersion is directly proportional to that of the dark matter halo. The relation is not a single power law: in the ATLAS3D analysis the mean relation breaks near 3×10^10 M☉, with M proportional to sigma^2.3 and sigma^4.7 at small and large sigma (Cappellari et al. 2013), and the velocity dispersion function of quiescent SDSS galaxies is remarkably flat at low sigma (Sohn et al. 2017). Cappellari (2016) reviews the structure and kinematics of early-type galaxies. Simulations must measure sigma the way a fibre does, and the radius matters: Horizon-AGN and NewHorizon reproduce the variety of velocity dispersion profile slopes seen in SAMI and CALIFA, and their stellar-mass dependence, at inner and outer radii (Han et al. 2024). Compare curves only with the same dimension (line of sight or three-dimensional), aperture and weighting for sigma, the same stellar mass definition and IMF, and the same population (quiescent or all galaxies).

sigma1.title: Central stellar surface density (Σ1) – mass relation
sigma1.paragraph: Sigma_1 is the stellar mass inside the inner 1 kpc divided by the area of that circle, plotted here against total stellar mass. It measures how dense a galaxy's core is and is used to follow the growth of the bulge. For SDSS central galaxies, Fang et al. (2013) found that galaxies quench once Sigma_1 crosses a threshold that grows with stellar mass as M^0.64, and that a dense bulge appears necessary but not sufficient to quench a galaxy fully. Since z=3, star-forming and quiescent galaxies occupy distinct linear relations between log Sigma_1 and log M whose slopes and scatter barely change while their normalisations decline, and quiescent galaxies have denser cores than star-forming galaxies of the same mass (Barro et al. 2017). Conselice (2014) reviews how galaxy structure evolves over cosmic time. Simulations link the core to the history of the gas: in zoom simulations a wet compaction event at about 10^9.5 M☉ is followed by depletion of the central 1 kpc and saturation of the stellar density there (Tacchella et al. 2016), and in IllustrisTNG, which retains too much cold gas in quenched galaxies compared with observations, Sigma_1 correlates tightly with black-hole mass (Ma et al. 2022). Because the 1 kpc aperture is small, curves are comparable only if the mass profile method (SED-based or colour-based mass-to-light ratio, treatment of seeing), the stellar mass definition, the IMF and the population (star-forming, quiescent or all) agree.

agnlf.title: AGN luminosity function
agnlf.paragraph: The AGN luminosity function counts active nuclei per unit comoving volume per dex of luminosity, either bolometric or in a stated band such as 2 to 10 keV. Its integral over luminosity is the luminosity density that powers black-hole growth. Hopkins et al. (2007) compiled quasar luminosity functions in the optical, soft and hard X-ray and near and mid-infrared, accounted for the observed column-density distributions and SED shapes, and found that a single bolometric function reproduces the observed functions in all bands, with the total luminosity density peaking at z=2.15±0.05. Shen et al. (2020) update this with a new SED model and extinction corrections: the normalisation falls towards high redshift and the bright-end slope is steeper at z>2, while the faint end at z>5 remains uncertain. Ueda et al. (2014) provide the X-ray luminosity function and absorption function from 4039 detections at 0<z<5. Hickox & Alexander (2018) review how obscuration hides much of the accretion, and Brandt & Alexander (2015) review cosmic X-ray surveys. Simulations differ widely: in six of them the function varies significantly, agrees with observations at z=0, and at higher redshift mostly produces too many AGN around 10^43 to 10^44 erg/s (Habouzit et al. 2021); TNG matches the low-redshift function but over-predicts the high-redshift one (Weinberger et al. 2018). Compare curves only with the same band and bolometric correction, the same obscuration treatment (intrinsic or observed) and the same comoving normalisation per dex.

bhad.title: Black-hole accretion rate density
bhad.paragraph: The black-hole accretion rate density is the mass accreted by black holes per unit time and comoving volume as a function of redshift. Observationally it is inferred from the AGN luminosity density by assuming a radiative efficiency, so it is the time derivative of the cosmic black-hole mass density. Madau & Dickinson (2014) show that the comoving rates of star formation and of central black-hole accretion follow a similar rise and fall, which they read as evidence for co-evolution, and Heckman & Best (2014) review what surveys of the contemporary Universe say about that link. Hopkins et al. (2007) integrate their bolometric quasar luminosity function to predict the relic black-hole mass density, and Shen et al. (2020) find that the cosmic black-hole mass density and mass function implied by their updated function are generally consistent with existing observations. Simulations are checked against this history: ASTRID is broadly consistent with empirical constraints on the time evolution of black-hole mass and accretion rate density (Ni et al. 2022), Horizon-AGN reproduces the redshift evolution of the black-hole mass density (Volonteri et al. 2016), and TNG tends to over-predict the high-redshift quasar luminosity function (Weinberger et al. 2018). Observed curves depend on the assumed radiative efficiency, the bolometric correction, the obscuration correction, and on whether the factor (1 minus efficiency) is applied, which is 0.046 dex at an efficiency of 0.1; compare only matched conventions, per comoving volume.

lambdar.title: Stellar spin parameter (λR) – mass relation
lambdar.paragraph: The spin parameter lambda_R is a proxy for the projected stellar angular momentum per unit mass, built from luminosity-weighted averages over the full two-dimensional velocity field, and evaluated here within the effective radius. Emsellem et al. (2007) introduced it with SAURON integral-field data to separate early-type galaxies into slow and fast rotators. In the MASSIVE and ATLAS3D samples of 370 early-type galaxies, Veale et al. (2017) find a strong correlation between lambda_e and stellar mass, with the average lambda_e falling from about 0.4 to below 0.1 with increasing mass, and almost no trend with environment at fixed mass. Cappellari (2016) reviews the structure and kinematics of early-type galaxies that this builds on. Simulations are tested against it as a population property: Illustris reproduces rotation properties similar to ATLAS3D, with low-mass ellipticals forming a smooth distribution of fast rotators and high-mass ones mostly slow rotators, in agreement with observations (Penoyre et al. 2017), and Magneticum ellipticals show the observed prevalence of fast and slow rotators (Schulze et al. 2018). Schulze et al. (2018) also show that the fast and slow dichotomy is enhanced in the edge-on plane of lambda_R and ellipticity, so the viewing angle matters. Curves are comparable only if the projection and orientation, the aperture and weighting, the statistic (mean or median), the population (early types only or all galaxies) and the stellar mass definition agree.

fslow.title: Slow-rotator fraction – mass relation
fslow.paragraph: The slow-rotator fraction is the share of early-type galaxies whose stellar rotation is weak, as a function of stellar mass, and it is one of the cleanest kinematic signatures of how massive galaxies assemble. The definition of a slow rotator has changed: Emsellem et al. (2007) separated the classes at lambda_R below or above 0.1 within the effective radius, while Emsellem et al. (2011), with a complete sample of 260 galaxies, introduced a criterion that depends on ellipticity, lambda_R below 0.31 times the square root of epsilon, and found that 14% of early types in the volume-limited ATLAS3D sample are slow rotators. In MASSIVE and ATLAS3D together, the slow-rotator fraction rises from about 10% to 90% with increasing stellar mass (Veale et al. 2017), and Cappellari (2016) reviews the dichotomy between the two classes. Simulations broadly reproduce the trend: Illustris ellipticals are mostly fast rotators at low mass and slow rotators at high mass in agreement with observations (Penoyre et al. 2017), Magneticum shows the observed prevalence (Schulze et al. 2018), and in EAGLE, where slow rotators are visually classified, quenching by AGN feedback precedes kinematic transformation in most of them (Lagos et al. 2021). Curves are comparable only if the slow-rotator criterion, the aperture, the projection, the stellar mass proxy and the parent population (early types or all galaxies) agree; a fraction among early types is not a fraction of all galaxies.

wp.title: Projected galaxy correlation function
wp.paragraph: The projected correlation function w_p(r_p) measures the excess probability of finding a galaxy pair at projected separation r_p, with the line-of-sight pair separation integrated up to a stated maximum. It is the standard clustering statistic for comparing simulated galaxies with redshift surveys and the data to which halo occupation models are fitted. In the SDSS DR7 main sample, Zehavi et al. (2011) measured it for volume-limited samples and found that the amplitude grows slowly with luminosity below L* and sharply above, that redder galaxies cluster more strongly and steeply at fixed luminosity, and that the trends are naturally understood within the LCDM and halo occupation framework. Wechsler & Tinker (2018) review how surveys and simulations constrain the galaxy-halo connection, and list its link to galaxy clustering among the open questions. EAGLE agrees very well with GAMA clustering when galaxies are binned by stellar mass, colour or luminosity, but low-mass red galaxies are clustered too strongly, partly through limited resolution, and the box is too small to test scales beyond a few Mpc (Artale et al. 2017). IllustrisTNG agrees well with SDSS at z~0.1 as a function of stellar mass and colour, apart from a mild excess for red galaxies of 10^9 to 10^10 M☉/h^2 (Springel et al. 2018). Curves are comparable only if the sample selection (luminosity threshold, stellar mass threshold or colour cut), the maximum line-of-sight integration, and the length unit (h^-1 Mpc here) agree; the SDSS records here integrate to 40 or 60 h^-1 Mpc and the EAGLE record to about 34.

hod.title: Halo occupation distribution
hod.paragraph: The halo occupation distribution gives the mean number of galaxies hosted by a halo as a function of halo mass, usually split into central and satellite galaxies. Berlind & Weinberg (2002) defined the framework through the probability that a halo of mass M contains N galaxies, together with the spatial distribution of galaxies within halos, and showed how different clustering statistics respond to it. Zheng et al. (2005) used a hydrodynamical simulation and a semi-analytic model to examine the separate contributions of central and satellite galaxies. Zehavi et al. (2011) fitted halo occupation models to SDSS clustering and found that the growth of clustering with luminosity reflects a shift in the minimum host halo mass. Wechsler & Tinker (2018) review the galaxy-halo connection as a test of galaxy formation models. In EAGLE and Illustris, low-mass halos in dense environments are more likely to host a central galaxy than those in sparse ones, and early-formed halos host fewer satellites (Artale et al. 2018), so the occupation is not a function of mass alone; EAGLE galaxies are found to inhabit similar halos to the observed GAMA galaxies (Artale et al. 2017). The records use different samples and mass definitions: SDSS luminosity-threshold samples with halo mass defined at 200 times the mean density, simulation samples ranked by stellar mass at fixed number density with M200 relative to the critical density. Compare only matched galaxy type (all, central or satellite), sample selection and halo mass definition.

lxm.title: X-ray luminosity–halo mass relation
lxm.paragraph: The X-ray luminosity–mass relation of groups and clusters links the luminosity of their hot gas to the mass M500c inside the radius enclosing 500 times the critical density. It is a sensitive probe of the gas content and of feedback, and it is used to turn X-ray surveys into mass estimates. For the 31 REXCESS clusters, Pratt et al. (2009) find power laws steeper than the self-similar expectation, with a systematic variation of gas content with mass as the primary driver, a scatter dominated by cool cores, and a scatter reduced by more than 50% when the central regions are excluded. Giodini et al. (2013) review scaling relations and the deviations from self-similarity. In simulations, the C-EAGLE clusters have soft-band luminosities in reasonable agreement with observed relations but too high central temperatures and larger-than-observed entropy cores (Barnes et al. 2017); cosmo-OWLS models with the right AGN feedback give realistic groups and clusters while others are too violent (Le Brun et al. 2014); and simulated relations are in general agreement with observations, with the mass-Y_X scaling the most robust and almost independent of the gas physics (Truong et al. 2018). Curves are comparable only if the X-ray band (bolometric or a soft band such as 0.1 to 2.4 keV), the treatment of the core (included or excised), the E(z) scaling, the aperture, the halo mass definition and how the mass was obtained (hydrostatic, Y_X-based, lensing, or true simulation mass) agree.

refs.cite: Giodini et al. 2013, Space Sci. Rev. 177, 247

ysz.title: Sunyaev–Zel'dovich signal–mass relation
ysz.paragraph: The Y_SZ-M500 relation connects the integrated thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich signal of a cluster, a measure of its hot-gas pressure, to its mass M500c. Arnaud et al. (2010) derived a universal pressure profile from the 33 REXCESS clusters, with masses between 10^14 and 10^15 M☉, and from it the expected relation for the spherically and the cylindrically integrated signal and for any aperture. Planck Collaboration (2011) combined all-sky Planck data with X-ray clusters and found the measured SZ signal in excellent agreement with X-ray-based predictions over the whole luminosity range, with no significant deviation from standard evolution. Planck Collaboration (2014) used a relation between mass and SZ signal calibrated to X-ray measurements for cluster counts, and found that possible biases in that relation and in the halo mass function are larger than the statistical errors; they allowed the X-ray mass to be biased low by zero to 30%. Mroczkowski et al. (2019) review the SZ effects as probes of galaxy clusters. Simulations are tested on the same relation: the C-EAGLE clusters have SZ properties in reasonable agreement with the observed relations (Barnes et al. 2017), and cosmo-OWLS models with suitable AGN feedback broadly reproduce the observed SZ flux among other properties (Le Brun et al. 2014). Curves are comparable only if the aperture (spherical or cylindrical), the E(z) scaling, the mass definition and mass estimator (hydrostatic, Y_X-based, lensing or true), and the cosmology and h-units agree.

refs.cite: Mroczkowski et al. 2019, Space Sci. Rev. 215, 17

colour.title: Galaxy colour–mass distribution
colour.paragraph: The colour-mass distribution shows the rest-frame g-r colour of galaxies against stellar mass. It is bimodal, with a blue cloud of star-forming galaxies and a red sequence of passive ones, and it is therefore a direct test of how and when galaxies quench. The bimodality in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey was first detected as a local minimum in the colour distribution, with the two peaks corresponding roughly to early and late types (Strateva et al. 2001), and Baldry et al. (2004) quantified it with double Gaussians in colour-magnitude space, finding that the transitions occur around 2×10^10 M☉. Blanton & Moustakas (2009) review the physical properties of nearby galaxies. In IllustrisTNG, once dust attenuation is included, the simulated g-r colours of galaxies between 10^9 and 10^12.5 M☉ agree excellently with SDSS, with a sharp transition at about 10^10.5 M☉ that is driven by black-hole feedback in its low-accretion state (Nelson et al. 2018). EAGLE produces a red sequence and a blue cloud with g-r colours within 0.1 magnitudes of those observed, but its blue cloud extends to somewhat higher luminosities and its passive fraction is modestly underestimated in massive galaxies (Trayford et al. 2015). These agreements hold only with dust models: intrinsic colours, which the CAMELS-TNG records here use, are not comparable with attenuated ones, and different dust models, the choice of one line of sight or all projections, the passband, and the population (all galaxies or centrals only) must also match.

elf.title: Emission-line luminosity function
elf.paragraph: The emission-line luminosity function counts galaxies per unit comoving volume per dex of the luminosity of one line, here H-alpha. H-alpha comes from gas ionised by young stars and traces recent star formation, but the luminosity depends on how it was obtained: with or without the neighbouring [NII] lines, and with or without a dust correction. Kennicutt & Evans (2012) review the techniques and calibrations for measuring star formation rates. The HiZELS narrow-band surveys give the function at z = 0.40, 0.84, 1.47 and 2.23, corrected for [NII] and for a constant 1 magnitude of extinction; Sobral et al. (2013) find a faint-end slope near -1.6 at all four epochs and a characteristic luminosity that rises by a factor of about ten from z = 0 to z = 2.2. Covelo-Paz et al. (2025) measure the observed, uncorrected function from JWST grism spectra of 1050 emitters at 3.7 < z < 6.7 and compare it with three simulations, finding good agreement at z of about 4 to 6 and that SPHINX lies below their function where the two overlap. Hirschmann et al. (2023) predict the H-alpha, [OIII]+H-beta and [OII] functions of IllustrisTNG from z of about 0 to 6, without dust attenuation outside H II regions, and compare them with dust-corrected observations. Compare curves only with the same line, the same dust treatment (observed, corrected by a fixed number of magnitudes or by the Balmer decrement, or modelled) and the same aperture; the 1 magnitude correction of Sobral et al. alone is 0.4 dex.
